title: Hide Artifacts: File/Path Exclusions
summary: File and Path Exclusions describes placing malicious files in locations that antivirus and other scanners are configured not to read. Scanning products exclude folders and file names to cut performance cost and to avoid breaking legitimate applications, and those exclusions are often hardcoded defaults rather than decisions made by the local administrator. Instead of changing tool settings, which tends to generate its own alerts, an adversary discovers the excluded paths and drops payloads there. The file is written normally and nothing is disabled, so tamper protection may never fire. Detection looks at what is created inside well known exclusion directories, at unusual child processes launched from them, and at the exclusion configuration itself, which should be reviewed and kept as narrow as the workload allows.

beginner.definition: Antivirus software scans files for signs of malware. Scanning everything all the time is slow, so administrators often exclude some folders. That means the antivirus skips them. An attacker who learns which folders are skipped can hide files there. The antivirus stays quiet because it never looks.
beginner.whyItMatters: Exclusions usually exist for good reasons, such as performance or application support. But they create blind spots. An attacker does not need to switch off the antivirus at all. Writing a file into a trusted, skipped folder is enough. Because nothing is disabled, the security settings still look normal. Reviewing exclusions and watching those folders is how you close this gap.
howItWorks: Administrators add exclusions so that the antivirus skips certain folders or file names.
These exclusions often exist to keep important applications working and to save time.
The attacker first looks for security software and learns which paths are excluded.
They then write their payload into one of those trusted folders that is skipped.
The scanners pass over that folder, so the new file is never inspected.
No security tool is disabled, so tamper alarms and configuration checks stay quiet.
beginner.example: Imagine a museum where guards patrol every room. To save time, the manager tells the guards to skip one storage corridor. The corridor is not locked, because it holds harmless supplies. Someone learns about this shortcut and leaves a stolen painting in that corridor. The guards walk past the open door every hour and see nothing, because they were told not to look. File path exclusions work the same way. Nothing is broken, and nobody switched off the guard.
takeaways: Antivirus exclusions create blind spots that an attacker can use.
A malicious file inside an excluded folder raises no alert by itself.
Review exclusions often and keep them as narrow as possible.

objectives: Explain what a scanner exclusion is and why organisations use one.
Describe how an attacker finds and abuses excluded file paths.
Explain why this behaviour differs from disabling a security tool outright.
Identify telemetry for newly created files inside excluded directories.
Recommend a practical process for reviewing an exclusion list.
